newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: In Korea, brinksmanship and blackmail obscure peace.
newsitem.headline: In Korea, brinksmanship and blackmail obscure peace.

text.p: If North Korea was just another Third World famine victim, transport planes with medicines and baby food might even now be flying mercy missions to Pyongyang.
Ships brimming with desperately-needed grain might be steaming to its ports.

Instead, while eyewitness reports of pot-bellied children emerge from communist North Korea, donor nations -- particularly the United States, South Korea and Japan -- are in a quandry over what to do.
Nobody wants North Koreans to starve to death, and few relish the prospect of the world's last Stalinist dictatorship imploding, spilling out refugees and possibly igniting war.

Yet during a visit to South Korea last week, U.S. defence secretary William Cohen made no secret of Washington's distaste for feeding a nation that, while begging for food, pours scarce resources into a 1.1 million-strong military and threatens South Korea with chemical-tipped missiles.
So while North Korea reports that children are dying of malnutrition -- the official toll stands at 134 -- donors are agonising not over how much aid to give, but how little.
The next move in this Cold War game of brinksmanship and blackmail comes on Wednesday.
On the first anniversary of an offer by U.S. President Bill Clinton and South Korean head of state Kim Young-sam for four-way peace talks, Pyongyang has said it will give an answer.

Washington and Seoul regard the talks as a forum for the two Koreas to hammer out a peace accord to replace a truce that ended the 1950-53 Korean War. China has been invited to sit on the sidelines with the United States.
North Korea wants massive food aid, diplomatic recognition from Washington and an easing of the U.S.-imposed trade embargo throttling its economy.
To try to secure these gains, its response to the talks offer is likely to be a qualified yes, according to officials and analysts in Seoul and Washington.
But the question is: does North Korea also want peace?

"North Korea is not too much interested in the four-way talks," said Yu Suk-ryul, a researcher at South Korea's foreign ministry think-tank. "But it is interested in the benefits from accepting the proposal."
"It will try to wring out all that it can during the negotiating process."
On Saturday, North Korea warned Washington and Seoul against using food aid as leverage to wrest security concessions.

The state-run Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) quoted a North Korean foreign ministry official as condemning what he described as "strange assertions" by Washington and Seoul which he felt stated that food aid to the North could only be discussed once four-way peace talks were opened.

"Raising such a condition is a dishonest and inhumanitarian behaviour aimed at abusing food aid as a political weapon and securing a concession from the DPRK in the security issue," KCNA quoted the official as saying.
"If they think that the food problem decides whether we accept the 'talks' or not, it would be a serious mistake," the official added.

To prod Pyongyang to make peace, Washington has eased its trade embargo to allow commercial grain sales to the North and, along with Seoul, has chipped in to a $95 million appeal by the World Food Programme to buy 200,000 tonnes of food.
South Korea is also allowing private rice donations.
Japan is holding back. One reason is public anger over charges that North Korea kidnapped a Japanese schoolgirl in 1977 and spirited her to Pyongyang.
Meanwhile, aid agencies say millions of people are in danger of starvation and several million tonnes of food is needed to avert catastrophe.

Beyond calculations over what concessions, if any, Pyongyang is likely to make during peace talks -- and how these should be rewarded -- are fears that events on the Korean peninsula are moving out of control.
Impending famine is shaking hopes of coaxing North Korea towards a "soft landing" -- a slow reform of its system leading to peaceful unification with the South over several decades.

"The cherished vision of a gradual and orderly drawing together of the two Koreas is today nothing more than a fantasy," wrote Nicholas Eberstadt, a U.S. specialist on North Korea, in the latest issue of Foreign Affairs magazine.
North Korea, he said, "is more likely to implode".
That prospect brought Cohen, and the Chairman of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff, General John Shalikashvili to Seoul last week to discuss emergency security plans.
Cohen warned Pyongyang any aggression would be "suicidal", resulting in "overwhelming damage and defeat".
